title: SYSK Selects: How The Black Panther Party Worked
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of the episode on how the Black Panther Party worked. Josh opens by framing the episode around the current struggle for civil rights and human rights. Hosts trace the Jim Crow-era background, Robert Williams and Negroes with Guns, and the founding of the Black Panther Party for Self Defense in Oakland by Huey Newton and Bobby Seal, with the Malcolm X influence and the Marxist, class-based analysis. They go through the Ten Point Program, the Black Panther newspaper, the branding and black leather look, copwatching patrols and the open-carry loophole that led to the Mulford Act signed by Reagan, and the role of women such as Kathleen Cleaver and Elaine Brown. They cover the survival programs (free breakfast, free medical clinics, Oakland Community School), the FBI's COINTELPRO campaign under J. Edgar Hoover, the December 1969 raid that killed Fred Hampton in Chicago, the internal split between Newton and Eldridge Cleaver and the Black Liberation Army, the Alex Rackley case and Bobby Seal's trial, Seal's Oakland mayoral run, the Panther 21 trial, and the party's legacy compared with Black Lives Matter. The episode ends with a listener mail about the rubber trade in Latin America.

segments.title: Opening framing from Josh
segments.summary: Josh introduces the Selects episode, framing the history of Black civil rights and human rights struggles as relevant to the present.

segments.title: Introduction and the FBI smear campaign
segments.summary: Hosts say they knew little about the Black Panthers and note that the negative image owes much to an FBI misinformation campaign. Hoover called the party the greatest threat to the country during the Vietnam War.

segments.title: Jim Crow background and Robert Williams
segments.summary: Context on Jim Crow-era conditions and police mistreatment of Black Americans. Robert Williams, an NAACP leader in North Carolina, wrote Negroes with Guns in 1965 advocating armed self-defense.

segments.title: Founding of the Black Panther Party and Malcolm X's influence
segments.summary: Bobby Seal and Huey Newton, college students in Oakland, founded the Black Panther Party for Self Defense. The group named itself after the panther image, favoring defense over aggression. Malcolm X's influence and cooperation with like-minded groups of any race are noted, along with the Marxist, class-based analysis of capitalism.

segments.title: The Ten Point Program
segments.summary: The hosts read the party's Ten Point Program, covering freedom, full employment, housing, education, exemption from military service, an end to police brutality, release of prisoners, fair trials by a jury of peers, and a UN-supervised plebiscite.

segments.title: Black Panther newspaper and branding
segments.summary: The party sold The Black Panther newspaper, which printed the Ten Point Program in every issue and grew to about 250,000 circulation. Its artwork, by Emory Douglas, and its black leather and beret look helped build the brand, which was tied to the Black is Beautiful movement.

segments.title: Copwatching patrols and the California open-carry law
segments.summary: Party members patrolled Oakland, observing police traffic stops while armed. They used California's open-carry law, which led to a 1967 legislative protest. Governor Ronald Reagan signed the Mulford Act, which closed the open-carry loophole.

segments.title: Women in the party and leadership roles
segments.summary: Women like Kathleen Cleaver and Elaine Brown held high positions, though most women were rank and file. Women also did armed patrols. The hosts say the party was still somewhat chauvinistic.
topics: women in the Black Panther Party

segments.title: Survival programs and the Oakland Community School
segments.summary: The party ran survival programs including a free breakfast program feeding about 20,000 children daily, free medical clinics, and the Oakland Community School, which ran from 1970 to 1982. Donations funded them, and the party called for boycotts of businesses that refused to contribute.

segments.title: COINTELPRO and alliances with white groups
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how Hoover saw the social programs as the greatest threat because they drew outside support. The party allied with white groups such as the Young Patriots, and Huey Newton publicly backed gay and lesbian rights in 1970.

segments.title: Newton's arrest, Cleaver's exile, and the Fred Hampton raid
segments.summary: Newton was jailed for killing a police officer, sparking the Free Huey campaign. Bobby Hutton was killed by police after a shootout in Oakland, and Eldridge Cleaver fled to Algeria. Fred Hampton, a Chicago leader, was killed in a December 1969 pre-dawn raid by Chicago police, which used an FBI-supplied informant's map. Around 90 shots were fired, and a 1970 coroner's jury ruled the deaths justifiable.

segments.title: Internal split, Black Liberation Army, and the Alex Rackley case
segments.summary: Newton and Cleaver became openly hostile, and factions fought each other. The Black Liberation Army split from the party in 1971. Alex Rackley was killed by party members in 1969, and Bobby Seal was tried for the murder and acquitted, which hurt public support.

segments.title: Decline, Seal's mayoral run, Panther 21, and legacy
segments.summary: Membership declined. Bobby Seal ran for mayor of Oakland and lost in a runoff. Seal was jailed for contempt in the Chicago Eight trial. The Panther 21 trial in New York ended in acquittals. The hosts discuss the party's legacy, the Clinton urban legend, and Eldridge Cleaver's claim about gang violence, plus lynching and police killing statistics and the comparison with Black Lives Matter.

segments.title: Listener mail on the rubber trade and sign-off
segments.summary: A listener adds to the rubber trade episode, noting the Peruvian Amazon Rubber Company's atrocities. The hosts sign off with listener contact details.
